research.topic: Loudest animal: sperm whale echolocation clicks measured at source levels up to 236 dB re 1 µPa (pp) at 1 m by Møhl et al. 2003 (JASA), recorded off Andenes, northern Norway, with a hydrophone array; monopulsed clicks ~100 µs long from the spermaceti organ (the whale's enormous nose). Blue whale calls 188–191 dB re 1 µPa (Frontiers in Marine Science 2021). Howler monkeys: loudest land animal, ~140 dB in air, audible ~5 km (Current Biology 2015; Nat Geo). Sperm whales dive beyond 2,000 m hunting squid, navigating by echolocation. Underwater and in-air decibels are not directly comparable; the on-screen bars say so.

myths.myth: The blue whale, the biggest animal, is the loudest.
myths.reality: Blue whale calls reach about 188 dB underwater; sperm whale clicks have been measured at 236 dB underwater — the loudest biological sound recorded.

landscape.our_gap: Loudest-animal lists are stock-footage countdowns; nobody puts the three decibel bars on screen with the water/air caveat, erases 'a roar' into a click, pins the Norwegian canyon where the record was recorded and drops a depth counter as a quiz.
